• Other names: Juncus grass, Creeping rush, Lesser creeping rush, Rush
  • Difficulty: easy to medium
  • Lighting: medium
  • pH: 5.5 – 8.0
  • GH: 0 – 18
  • Temperature: 20 – 26 °C (68 – 79 °F)
  • Substrate: nutrient-rich
  • Can float: no
  • Growth form: stem
  • Can be grown emersed: yes
  • Growth rate: moderate (submersed), fast (emersed)
  • Placement: midground
  • Size: 10 – 40 cm (4 – 16 inches)
  • Fertilizers: not needed to low
  • CO2: not needed to low
  • Propagation: cut stem, new growth or lateral shoots
  • Colour: light green

The genus Juncus includes more than 200 species. Only Juncus repens has been found to be a good aquarium plant; all other species of the genus are suitable only as pond plants.

Juncus repens has a relatively limited distribution range. It is found along the Gulf of Mexico coast and the Atlantic coast of the Southeast United States (Alabama, Arkansas, Delaware, Florida, Georgia, Louisiana, Maryland, Mississippi, North Carolina, Oklahoma, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas and Virginia), in southeastern Mexico, and in western Cuba.

Juncus repens occurs in two forms, terrestrial and aquatic. It is abundant in and slightly out of very shallow water in swamps, ponds, bogs, lakes, ditches and slow-moving streams, and in moist loamy soil along the edges of woods.

Water and waterlogged conditions are well known to be associated with the presence of Juncus species.

Juncus repens can thrive in a variety of tank sizes. Keeping it in nano tanks may be possible only in low-tech tanks; otherwise it may grow fast, uncontrollably and even become invasive. The recommended minimum tank size is 10 gallons (~40 litres).

As it can grow emersed or submersed, it is also a good choice for garden ponds, terrariums and paludariums.

Juncus repens is easy to care for and adaptable, but the foliage must be trimmed from time to time to stop it overrunning the tank. Growth rate depends strongly on light intensity, nutrient availability and CO2.

Under low light, or until it takes hold, it is not a rapid grower; it may take several weeks to see growth. Under optimal conditions with high light it grows so rapidly that shoots need constant, aggressive pruning with curved scissors to keep a short, compact, grass-like form. Kept trimmed, it forms a nice carpet, but this is time-consuming. Without regular pruning, shoots reach the water surface; overgrowth is not a problem if a jungle look is desired.

Partial water changes are crucial, as they add micronutrients to the water and improve growth rate.

Planting

Thanks to its size and bushy appearance, it suits the midground. Use a substrate 5 – 7 cm (2 – 3 inches) deep to ease rooting.

  • Untie the bunch and divide it into several portions.
  • Disinfect or quarantine the plantlets (if not grown in vitro).
  • Place individual stems into the enriched substrate, about 5 – 8 cm (2 – 3 inches) apart to prevent overcrowding and shading.
  • Plant stems about 2.5 cm (1 inch) deep.
  • Avoid placing it near tall plants that shade it.
  • Avoid placing it too close to the glass, which limits its bushy growth.
  • Do not glue it onto driftwood or anything else; it will not survive.

Propagation

Juncus repens proliferates: stems and leaves produce new plants vegetatively until the plant becomes a branching tangle. Underwater stolons/runners bear independent daughter plants that cover the substrate quickly. Daughter plants can be cut off and replanted or left alone. You can also cut the top of the plant or cut at each point where roots emerge.

Dry start method

Instead of filling the tank with water after planting, add only enough water to reach the surface of the lowest part of the substrate. Use tweezers to plant Juncus repens and spread it over the substrate. Cover the tank with cling wrap to increase humidity. After about 5 – 8 weeks the tank can be flooded. This method provides unlimited CO2 at no cost and allows growing the plant even before cycling the tank.

Temperature: Juncus repens tolerates and thrives in a wide range of temperatures, even cooler water such as 10 °C (50 °F). However, 20 – 26 °C (68 – 79 °F) is ideal.

pH: the plant prefers pH 5.5 – 8.0; neutral pH is more suitable. Even though it is hardy, monitor pH regularly with an accurate test kit. pH affects nutrient uptake and is therefore a significant factor for growth.

Hardness: it is resilient and grows in soft to hard water without problems (0 to 18 GH).

Lighting: Juncus repens thrives in medium light (30 – 50 PAR). It tolerates low light only at the higher end of low light; if the light is really low, it will not succeed. Bright light causes faster, bushier growth with many runners, and a reddish tint as the plant nears the surface. Low light triggers upward growth and very slow growth. Provide about 8 – 10 hours of bright light daily with a quality aquarium LED or another suitable light source, and watch for algae and adjust the light accordingly.

Substrate: it is a heavy root-feeder and needs a nutrient-rich substrate. In sand or gravel, supplement regularly with root tabs. Recommended substrates: ADA Amazonia aqua soil, Carib Sea Eco-Complete, Seachem Fluorite.

CO2: it can grow without CO2 injection. With high light, however, CO2 and nutrients must be balanced, otherwise algae will quickly cover the tank. If CO2 is injected, provide more light and make sure fertilization needs are met.

Fertilization: liquid fertilizers are optional in low-tech tanks. Although the plant has a large root system, it also feeds from the water column and responds favourably to liquid fertilizers.

If shrimp are kept with it: a high level of CO2 and copper (most fertilizers contain copper) is extremely dangerous to shrimp.

Juncus repens suits community tanks with small peaceful fish and invertebrates that will not rip the leaves apart.

  • Small fish such as Otocinclus catfish, pygmy Cory catfish, ember tetra, neon tetra, green fire tetra, cardinal tetra, Celestial Pearl danio, zebra danio and platies.
  • Dwarf shrimp (Red Cherry, Blue Velvet, Snowball, Crystal Red, Caridina cf. babaulti, Blue Tiger, Malawa, Blue Bolt, Amano, ghost, bamboo, vampire shrimp, etc.). Basically any shrimp can be kept with it.
  • Snails (ramshorn, nerite, Malaysian trumpet, Japanese trapdoor, mystery snails, etc.).

It is compatible with most plants and animals that prefer low light. However, some snails and herbivorous fish such as plecos, goldfish, cichlids, rosy barbs, silver dollars and tilapia are likely to eat it.

It is a good choice for freshwater crab and crayfish tanks, animals notorious for destroying planted tanks; here it should not be a problem. However, do not keep it with most crayfish or freshwater crabs, which will likely tear the foliage and uproot the plant. Also avoid aggressive fish known as plant devourers, such as Texas cichlids, Jack Dempsey, Red Devil and oscars.

Description

Juncus repens is a stem plant growing in a rosette form with rhizomatous growth for rapid clonal reproduction. It is a perennial herbaceous flowering plant in the rush family Juncaceae. It was first described by the French botanist André Michaux. The name Juncus comes from the Latin 'jungo', 'to join or unite'; repens means 'crawling'.

  • Size: 10 – 40 cm tall; leaves narrow, flexible and thin (about 3 mm wide).
  • Rhizome: short and cespitose, but the plant can cover a large area through vegetative shoots on prostrate stems with long internodes.
  • Stem: lax and creeping, producing new tufts of leaves; appears as a flat, black runner.
  • Leaves: grass-like; usually light green, turning reddish under very high light.
  • Flowers: in dense heads; in nature flowering runs from June to October. Flowers are small (about 5 mm) and elliptical, with rusty or straw-coloured tepals enclosing the fertile stamens and gynoecium.
  • Roots: adventitious, developing along the lower parts of the stem.
  • Seeds: 0.3 – 1.5 mm long, usually ellipsoid to ovoid, sometimes tailed.

Common problems

  • Emersed to submersed transition: may cause the green foliage to melt, but the plant recovers once fully settled. Be patient.
  • Algae: the plant is susceptible to algae, especially with excessive light and plentiful nutrients. Adjust light intensity, change water regularly and introduce algae eaters.
  • Relocation: the root system is large and the stem easily breaks; remove it slowly and carefully or a big part of the substrate will be pulled up.
  • Overgrowth: under high light and CO2 it grows fast and needs regular trimming; lowering the light also slows it.
  • Extremely slow growth: caused by inadequate nutrients or light; improving these restores growth.

Benefits

  • Decoration: its shape suits jungle aquascapes; untrimmed, it sends long shoots in different directions.
  • Prevents gas pockets: the well-developed root system helps break up anaerobic pockets in the substrate (hydrogen sulfide, H2S, smells like rotten eggs and can be dangerous to fish and shrimp).
  • Oxygenation: helps generate oxygen in the water.
  • Hiding place: provides cover and shade for invertebrates and small fish.
  • Foraging place: a source of biofilm, an ideal first food for newly hatched fry and shrimplets.
  • Not allelopathic: according to a study, it is not highly allelopathic and does not suppress other plants with chemicals.
